https://aa.com.tr/en/world/us-charge-5-f.text: RSS Diary Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 World US charge 5 for alleged Russian intelligence assassination plots 2 Cubans, Venezuelan among those accused of targeting Russian dissidents in US, Europe Mariam Ashalem De Andres 16 September 2026 • Update : 16 September 2026 İSTANBUL US authorities charged five people accused of working with Russian intelligence services on alleged plots to surveil and assassinate Russian dissidents and carry out attacks in the US and Europe, according to an indictment. “These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said in a statement Tuesday. The defendants were identified as Russian nationals Yuri Khrameev, 63, his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both 35, and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, 22. All were charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, while the elder Khrameev, Suarez and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. All remain at large, according to the US Justice Department. The indictment alleges that the network, described by prosecutors as the Russian Intelligence Services Network, had operated since at least 2024 and targeted Russian dissidents and defectors in the US and Europe. One alleged plot took place during July and August, when Suarez and Castro allegedly recruited a Brooklyn resident to conduct surveillance of two locations associated with a prominent Russian dissident believed to be living in the Washington, DC, area. The recruit was allegedly offered between $1,000 and $1,500 to photograph and record the locations, while prosecutors said another $40,000 was offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target. The indictment also alleges that members of the network coordinated attacks in Europe, including operations in the Czech Republic and Lithuania in 2024, targeting infrastructure in countries viewed as supporting Ukraine. Durruthy allegedly coordinated travel and logistics for participants in those operations, while prosecutors described Suarez as a recruiter for the network. US authorities said the investigation was conducted by the FBI's New York and Washington field offices, with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations. https://www.politico.eu/article/quebec-p.text: Quebec’s separatist premier says that he will boycott the EU-Canada summit that opens in Montreal on Thursday, warning European leaders that deals struck there without his government’s consent may not be applied in the country’s second-biggest province. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon confirmed his absence late Wednesday in an open letter to the European delegation, which he posted on X . His announcement followed two days of public sparring with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney over Ottawa’s refusal to let him address the summit. “This dynamic creates uncertainty as to the application of the agreements you could negotiate during the summit,” he wrote in French. Advertisement Advertisement In the letter, St-Pierre Plamondon says Ottawa has “decided to sideline Quebec” from the talks. He says this leaves his government with “neither a chair at the negotiating table nor the opportunity to speak,” even though the summit is on Quebec soil. Under Canada’s federal system, he argued, the provinces implement international agreements that fall within their powers. Without Quebec’s consent, a deal that runs against its interests “will simply not be implemented,” he wrote. He also accused Ottawa of withholding “critical information” on the negotiations. He offered to meet European leaders “in the near future, in a more opportune context.” He will send Quebec’s chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to the summit in his place. Carney said Wednesday his office had offered the premier the honor of welcoming the Commission president to Montreal, and a seat at the head table. “I hope he will reconsider,” he said. On Tuesday, the prime minister had accused St-Pierre Plamondon of choosing to “leave an empty chair again.” The row has soured the upbeat mood around the summit, which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a milestone. Leaders will launch an “ Alliance for the Future ,” a framework for shared prosperity and economic security. St-Pierre Plamondon’s letter says many of its topics fall under Quebec’s responsibility, including health, education and natural resources. Advertisement Advertisement The premier has also pursued his own contacts with European leaders. He spoke by phone with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday, and said the two had agreed on a possible meeting in France in the coming weeks. At working level, ties have held so far, and officials describe the relationship as constructive. Hélène Drainville, Quebec’s delegate general in Brussels, told POLITICO last week that Quebec was in talks with the European Investment Bank and the Commission, and that “all the signals are green.” Carney, Costa and von der Leyen are due to hold a joint press conference on Friday.
